sections.label: Optimal OFR amount estimate
sections.summary: MAS estimates the optimal amount of OFR it needs is currently around 65% to 75% of GDP.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: The optimal amount of OFR that MAS estimates it needs is currently around 65% to 75% of GDP.

sections.label: Current OFR stock level
sections.summary: The stock of OFR has grown to S$566 billion, about 111% of GDP as at the third quarter of 2021.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Today, the stock of OFR has grown to S$566 billion, or about 111% of GDP as at the third quarter of 2021.

sections.label: Transfer to reach optimal range
sections.summary: Bringing OFR to 75% of GDP would require about S$185 billion eventually transferred to the Government.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: For example, if we want to bring the current level of OFR to the upper end of the optimal range, or 75% of GDP, about S$185 billion of OFR will have to be eventually transferred to the Government.

sections.label: Reserves Management Government Securities amendments
sections.summary: The Bill amends the MAS Act to let MAS subscribe to a new non-marketable security, Reserves Management Government Securities, for transferring unneeded OFR.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: The Bill sets out legislative amendments that will introduce powers in the MAS Act for MAS to subscribe for a new type of non-marketable security issued by the Government solely to facilitate such transfers of OFR that is not needed for MAS' mandate.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: This new security is called Reserves Management Government Securities (RMGS).

sections.label: RMGS net issuance limit
sections.summary: The Bill introduces a separate RMGS net issuance limit of S$580 billion, of which about S$185 billion is for phased transfers to the Government.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: The Bill will introduce within the GSA a separate net issuance limit for RMGS, which will be S$580 billion.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: Of this amount, about S$185 billion represents the amount which MAS will have to transfer to the Government in phases to bring the level of OFR back to the optimal range.

sections.label: Monthly RMGS publication
sections.summary: For transparency, MAS will publish the outstanding RMGS amounts each month.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: For transparency, MAS will publish the outstanding RMGS amounts each month.

sections.label: Government borrowing for non-spending purposes
sections.summary: The Government's borrowing approach is unchanged, for non-spending purposes, except SINGA which finances nationally significant infrastructure spending.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Finance (Mr Lawrence Wong)
sentences.text: The Government's approach towards borrowing remains unchanged – the Government's borrowings is for non-spending purposes with the exception of the recently introduced SINGA to finance spending on nationally significant infrastructure.

sections.label: EDB 2020 investment commitments
sections.summary: In 2020, EDB attracted $17 billion in direct investment commitments, keeping up with the trajectory for inbound direct investments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: In 2020, despite being an uncertain and challenging year, EDB was able to attract direct investment commitments of $17 billion, very much keeping up to the trajectory for inbound direct investments.

sections.label: MAS official foreign reserves increase
sections.summary: MAS held S$566 billion of OFR as at November 2021, up from S$479 billion in December 2020.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: The Minister has just mentioned that the MAS, as at November 2021, holds S$566 billion of OFR.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: This is quite a significant increase from the year before of S$479 billion in December 2020.

sections.label: Optimal OFR level of GDP
sections.summary: MAS determines the optimal level of the OFR should be about 65% to 75% of Singapore's GDP.

sentences.speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
sentences.text: MAS determines that the optimal level of the OFR should be about 65% to 75% of Singapore's GDP.

sections.label: Transfer of excess OFR to GIC
sections.summary: The Bill will allow transfer of OFRs in excess of what MAS requires for monetary policy to the GIC for management.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The Bill will allow the transfer of official foreign reserves, or OFRs, in excess of what is required by MAS for the conduct of monetary policy to the GIC for management.

sections.label: Clause 15A cap and resolution
sections.summary: Clause 15A indicates a cap of $580 billion, which under article 144(a) of the Constitution requires a Parliamentary resolution to overturn.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Yet clause 15A indicates a cap aggregate amount of $580 billion, which by article 144(a) of the Constitution, requires a Parliamentary resolution to overturn.

sections.label: Singapore headline inflation rate
sections.summary: Singapore's headline inflation rate touched 3.8% in November, the highest in more than eight years.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Singapore's headline inflation rate, as we discussed earlier during Question Time, touched 3.8% in November, the highest in more than eight years.

sections.label: US currency manipulator watch list
sections.summary: In 2019 the US Treasury first placed Singapore on a watch list for currency manipulators, maintained in April last year's iteration.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In 2019, the US Treasury first placed Singapore on a watch list for currency manipulators, a position that it maintained in its latest iteration released in April last year.

sections.label: Gradual Singapore dollar appreciation
sections.summary: The speaker suggests the Government consider whether gradual Singapore dollar appreciation might eventually be warranted, mitigating the excess OFR problem.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: If so, perhaps the Government will consider whether a true gradual appreciation of the Singapore dollar – which would in turn indirectly mitigate much of the excess OFR problem that is a major motivation behind this Bill – might eventually be warranted, especially for an economy at our current stage of development.

sections.label: MAS printing Singapore dollars
sections.summary: The Bill lets MAS subscribe to RMGS, potentially allowing the Government to accumulate foreign reserves by having MAS print Singapore dollars.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: As the amount of Government deposits equals the excess savings in our economy, the accumulation of foreign reserves is limited by the size of the excess savings as envisaged by Dr Goh.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: However, this Bill opens up the possibility of the Government accumulating foreign reserves through simply getting MAS to print Singapore dollars.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: This is effected through clause 2 of this Bill, which deletes and substitutes section 23(6) of the MAS Act, to allow the MAS to subscribe to the Reserve Management Government Securities (RMGS) although section 23(5) states that MAS shall not directly subscribed for any securities issued by the Government or any public authority.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: In layman's term, while MAS cannot do quantitative easing in the past, it can potentially do so – and I say potentially, not necessarily so – if this Bill is passed.

sections.label: Foreign reserves and OFR limit
sections.summary: Foreign reserve increases in 2020 and 2021 totalling over $180 billion pushed the OFR to $566 billion by end 2021, exceeding the $325 billion limit.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The large foreign reserve increases in 2020 and 2021, amounting to more than $180 billion in total, pushed the OFR to $566 billion by end 2021, far exceeding the targeted OFR limit of $325 billion.

sections.label: Reserve Management Government Securities IOUs
sections.summary: The Bill allows the Government to create Reserve Management Government Securities, a new class of IOU, to pay for foreign reserves transferred from MAS to GIC.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: As the Government has no money to pay, we are debating this Bill today to allow the Government to pay with an IOU.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Hence, this Bill allows the Government to create a new class of IOU, called the Reserve Management Government Securities (RMGS) to pay for foreign reserves to be transferred from MAS to GIC.

sections.label: RMGS limit size concern
sections.summary: The $580 billion RMGS limit proposed in the Bill is far too large and is not annual.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: The $580 billion limit for the RMGS proposed in the Bill is far too large and is not on an annual basis.

sections.label: Financial assets and reserves growth
sections.summary: Government-managed financial assets belonging to Singaporeans grew from $1.35 trillion in 2019 to $1.4 trillion in 2020, with reserves rising despite a $53 billion drawdown.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: According to the GFS for Fiscal Year 2020, the total financial assets managed by the Government and belonging to all Singaporeans have grown from $1.35 trillion in 2019 to $1.4 trillion in 2020.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
sentences.text: Our reserves have continued to increase in 2020 despite the largest drawdown of $53 billion in the history of our nation to combat the COVID-19 pandemic.

sections.label: MAS OFR transfer mechanism
sections.summary: The amendment Bill's new mechanism transfers the MAS OFR through subscription to Reserves Management Government Securities issued by the Government.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The new mechanism proposed under the amendment Bill overcomes this constraint by providing for the transfer of the MAS OFR through a subscription to the Reserves Management Government Securities (RMGS) issued by the Government.

sections.label: Net foreign assets increase
sections.summary: High private savings and the constitutional budget balance requirement have steadily increased Singapore's net foreign assets over the years.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: On the first question, Singapore's high private savings rate alongside the constitutional requirement that the Government must achieve at least budget balance over its term of office has meant that the country's holdings of net foreign assets – that is the excess of our gross assets over our gross liabilities – have steadily increased over the years.

sections.label: Real exchange rate 1985
sections.summary: A statistical analysis of quarterly data from 1983 to 2018 showed the real exchange rate was high around 1985, when Singapore had its recession.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Broadly speaking, a statistical analysis done with data quarterly from 1983 to 2018 has shown that, largely speaking, around about 1985, which was when Singapore experienced its recession, the real exchange rate was high.

sections.label: MAS OFR safeguards
sections.summary: MAS foreign exchange intervention accumulates OFR, and the amendment Bill's safeguards prevent de facto money finance of fiscal policy.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In accordance with the MAS exchange rate monetary policy framework, its intervention in the foreign exchange market to dampen these pressures and keep the nominal effective exchange rate of the Singapore dollar within the policy band and conceptually that means trying to aim for what you think is the equilibrium real exchange rate, has led to a steady accumulation of OFR.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The explanatory brief put up by MAS at the First Reading of the amendment Bill has been at pains to make clear that there are safeguards to ensure that the new mechanism to be put in place does not lead to de facto money finance fiscal policy, that is, to let the central bank lend money to the Government to finance its spending and fiscal deficits.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: First, the amendment Bill requires that MAS can subscribe to RMGS solely for the purpose of facilitating the transfer of OFR and that its subscription does not compromise MAS' ability to achieve medium-term price stability.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Second, MAS will only be able to use its foreign currency asset to subscribe to RMGS.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The safeguards in the MAS (Amendment) Bill will complement the existing safeguard in the Government Security Act under which the Government proceeds from borrowing, can only be used for investment and market development purposes.

sections.label: Fiscal prudence and reserves deployment
sections.summary: The policy mix lets Singapore stay fiscally prudent, free MAS to focus on price stability, and deploy excess reserves to optimise returns.

sentences.speaker: Prof Hoon Hian Teck (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: With this policy mix, we can continue to exercise fiscal prudence, ensuring that we have the fiscal resources to pay for our recurrent spending and thus free MAS to focus on its function of maintaining medium-term price stability without facing the pressure of monetary financing.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: These amendments will help in the deployment of reserves that are in excess of baseline Official Foreign Reserves (OFR) to optimise returns for Singapore.

sections.label: MAS Official Foreign Reserves position
sections.summary: MAS states it maintains Official Foreign Reserves of at least 65% of GDP, which it deems sufficient to defend against speculative pressures.

sentences.speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: One, today MAS has a stated position of maintaining OFR of at least 65% of GDP to which it deems sufficient to defend against speculative pressures.

sections.label: Transferring excess reserves to GIC
sections.summary: The passage asks whether a sweeping mechanism should transfer excess reserves to GIC once Official Foreign Reserves reach a threshold such as 70%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Should a sweeping mechanism be imposed so that excess reserves can be transferred to GIC once the OFR reaches a threshold, say 70%?

sections.label: Reviewing the 65% threshold
sections.summary: The passage asks how the 65% threshold was derived and whether it should be reviewed or based on past capital outflows.

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: How was the 65% threshold being derived and should it be reviewed or should the OFR be multiples of the highest annual outflow of capital which Singapore had experienced in the past decade?

sections.label: MAS foreign reserves growth
sections.summary: Since 2016, foreign reserves managed by MAS have grown by an average of 11% each year, outpacing GDP growth.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Since 2016, foreign reserves managed by MAS have grown by an average of 11% each year, outpacing our GDP growth.

sections.label: MAS reserves sufficiency since 2019
sections.summary: Since 2019, MAS has said it does not need more than 65% of GDP in foreign reserves to maintain medium-term price stability.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Since 2019, MAS has said that it does not need more than 65% of GDP in foreign reserves to achieve its goal of maintaining medium-term price stability.

sections.label: MAS transfer to GIC
sections.summary: In 2019 MAS transferred $45 million to the Government for GIC to invest, and stated foreign reserves held by the Government are available in an extreme adverse scenario.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: In 2019, when MAS transferred $45 million to the Government for GIC to invest, MAS stated, "In the event of an extreme adverse scenario, the foreign reserves held by the Government are also available to ensure that MAS operations are not compromised." Can the Minister share how foreign reserves held by GIC and Temasek would be availed to MAS in the event of such an extreme adverse scenario?

sections.label: Limit on foreign reserves acceptance
sections.summary: Section 15A(2) of the amended Act limits the Government from accepting more than $580 billion of foreign reserves from MAS.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Section 15A(2) of the amended Act limits the Government from accepting more than $580 billion of foreign reserves from MAS.

sections.label: Optimal OFR amount
sections.summary: The optimal OFR amount needed to support MAS' mandate is currently defined as being at least 65% of GDP.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: First, the optimal OFR amount needed to support MAS' mandate is currently defined as being at least 65% of GDP.

sections.label: RMGS limit and maturity
sections.summary: The passage asks the Minister for the RMGS limit and the maturity period or duration of issued RMGS bonds, and notes intervention is needed if the OFR falls below 65%.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: Can the Minister share what is the RMGS limit and what is the maturity period or duration of the issued RMGS bonds?

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: This is meant to be an additional safeguard against monetary financing.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: However, in the case where the OFR falls below 65%, there will be a need for intervention.

sections.label: Monthly RMGS holdings publication
sections.summary: MAS' total RMGS holdings will be published monthly for transparency.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
sentences.text: In addition, MAS' total RMGS holdings will be published monthly for transparency.

sections.label: OFR adequacy and transfer
sections.summary: MAS assessed that an OFR of 65% to 75% of GDP is adequate, and OFR above this amount will be transferred to the Government to be managed separately.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Based on these considerations, MAS has, therefore, assessed that the OFR of 65% to 75% of GDP is adequate to meet its needs and OFR above this amount will then be transferred to the Government to be managed separately.

sections.label: MAS autonomy over monetary policy
sections.summary: MAS retains autonomy over monetary policy because MAS, not the Government, initiates the subscription of RMGS.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: With the introduction of RMGS, MAS continues to retain autonomy over monetary policy because it is MAS, not the Government, that initiates the subscription of RMGS.

sections.label: RMGS holdings and Sing dollar liquidity
sections.summary: MAS' accumulation of RMGS will not impact Sing dollar liquidity or sterilisation activities, and MAS will publish its RMGS holdings monthly.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Basically, MAS' accumulation of RMGS on its balance sheet will not impact Sing dollar liquidity and by extension, MAS' sterilisation activities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: On the frequency of published data, MAS will publish its RMGS holdings on a monthly basis.

sections.label: Sizing the $580 billion limit
sections.summary: The $580 billion limit is sized based on the OFR amount MAS needs to transfer and the expected pace of future OFR accumulation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: As I explained in my earlier speech, the $580 billion limit is sized based on two factors: one, the amount of OFR that MAS currently needs to transfer to the Government to bring the level of OFR in MAS back to its optimal amount; and two, the expected pace of OFR accumulation in future years.

sections.label: RMGS issued with 20-year tenor
sections.summary: All RMGS will be issued by the Government with a 20-year tenor, aligned with GIC's long-term investment horizon.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: As such, all RMGS will be issued by the Government with a 20-year tenor, which is aligned with GIC's long-term investment horizon.

sections.label: MAS redemption and transfer prohibition
sections.summary: MAS may redeem RMGS before maturity at par to meet OFR needs, and clause 15B(2)(a) prohibits transfers of RMGS holdings without the Minister for Finance's consent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Should such a situation arise, MAS will have the right to redeem the RMGS before maturity at par – meaning at full face value of the RMGS regardless of market conditions – to meet its OFR needs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: With the Government standing fully behind all the RMGS, we do not envisage that MAS will need to transfer its RMGS holdings to other entities to raise funds from the market.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: That is why clause 15B(2)(a) of the Bill, which Mr Saktiandi referred to, prohibits MAS’ transfers of RMGS holdings to other entities without consent from the Minister for Finance.

sections.label: GIC investing transferred OFR
sections.summary: How GIC will invest the transferred OFR is not expected to deviate from existing practice because such transfers have happened since GIC's formation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: In short, how GIC will invest the transferred OFR is not expected to deviate from existing practice because such transfers have been happening since the formation of GIC.

sections.label: OFR transfers and NIRC impact
sections.summary: Transfers of OFR not needed by MAS to the Government, enabled by RMGS, should slightly raise the NIRC over the long term.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: The transfers of OFR not needed by MAS to the Government, as enabled by RMGS, should have a slight positive impact on the NIRC over the long term.

sections.label: Spending as share of GDP
sections.summary: From 2006 to 2010, spending was about 15% of GDP.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Just as a comparison from 2006 to 2010, our spending was about 15% of GDP.

sections.label: Reserve information disclosure policy
sections.summary: MAS will review and release more useful information, but will not fully disclose how much reserves Singapore has, as reserves are a strategic asset.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: A lot of information is out there for serious analysts to understand how reserve management is done in Singapore and we will review and continue to see how we can put out more useful information to inform the public.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: But we do maintain the view that it is not in Singapore's interest to put out the full information on how much reserves we have.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: The reserves are ultimately a strategic asset against a whole range of emergency contingency scenarios.

sections.label: Bill, RMGS safeguards and reserves
sections.summary: The Bill creates a more sustainable mechanism for MAS to transfer OFR to the Government for GIC management, with safeguards tightly limiting RMGS use.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: A whole range of contingency scenarios and emergencies for which we will not know how much resources we need to respond.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: So, we believe that it is still in our national interest to maintain this strategic asset, not to have to disclose everything fully, but to have some discretion on our part and to be able to use these resources decisively and effectively when such an emergency arises.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: In summary, Sir, this Bill creates a more sustainable mechanism to facilitate MAS' transfer of OFR above what it requires to the Government for longer-term management by GIC.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: As I have repeatedly highlighted, safeguards will be put in place to circumscribe tightly the issuance and subscription of RMGS by the Government and MAS respectively, so that RMGS is used only for its intended purpose.

sections.label: Transfer amounts and remaining reserves
sections.summary: Transferring about $200 billion to GIC using the RMGS limit would still leave $380 billion.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: Because when he described that this round, we probably have to transfer $200 billion, use up the RMGS limit, about $200 billion dollars to transfer the assets to GIC, we are still left with $380 billion.

sections.label: Reserve threshold and Parliament approval
sections.summary: MAS estimates $580 billion as a sensible threshold for the next few years, and if reached, the Government must justify raising the limit for Parliament and President to approve.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: So, it can go either way because you may have appreciating pressures, you may have depreciating pressures, and MAS will have to intervene accordingly in order to maintain price stability.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: But we have put in our best estimates and we think that $580 billion is a sensible figure for the next few years.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Should that threshold be reached, then, as I mentioned, we will come back to Parliament to explain why we might need more, why we might have to raise the limit and it is for the Government to justify the case and for Parliament and President to approve.

sections.label: Reserves accumulation per year
sections.summary: The speaker says reserves are probably accumulating at about $30 to $50 billion a year, though unsure of the number.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: Then, you will be talking about $70 billion accumulation of reserves every year.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
sentences.text: I do not know the number, but probably, currently, we are accumulating at about $30 to $50 billion a year, right?

sections.label: MAS excess OFR and RMGS
sections.summary: Without RMGS, MAS would transfer excess OFR to the Government with a corresponding reduction in Government deposits, but slow deposit accumulation prevents this.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Under present circumstances, without RMGS, MAS will transfer its excess OFR to the Government and there will be a corresponding reduction in Government deposits.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: But because the pace in which the Government deposits is accumulating has been quite slow because we are running smaller fiscal surpluses, they will not be able to do the corresponding reduction in Government deposits and that is why this new mechanism allows MAS to use its excess OFR to subscribe to RMGS.

sections.label: MAS subscribing to RMGS
sections.summary: MAS first transfers excess OFR with a corresponding reduction in Government deposits, and is now proposed to use excess OFR to subscribe to RMGS, with no new money created.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: Like I said, in the first instance, it is done through a transfer of excess OFR and corresponding reduction in Government deposits; but in the second instance, we are proposing for MAS to use its excess OFR to subscribe to the RMGS.

sentences.speaker: Mr Lawrence Wong
sentences.text: There is no creation of new money in this process.
